title: Ethiopian Banking Law and Regulation
subtitle: Who regulates Ethiopian banks, under which laws, and what the prudential and conduct rules require day to day
summary: A plain-language map of Ethiopian banking regulation after the 2024 to 2025 reforms, from the new NBE and Banking Business proclamations to capital, exposure, provisioning and KYC rules.
audience: All bank staff, including new entrants, branch and operations staff, and anyone moving into compliance, risk, audit or credit. No prerequisites.
objectives: Describe the structure of the Ethiopian financial sector and the roles of the NBE, ECMA, the Financial Intelligence Service and the deposit insurance fund
Name the main proclamations and directives a bank operates under and what each covers
Explain in plain terms the capital, liquidity, large exposure, related-party, investment and provisioning rules and why they exist
Apply consumer protection, KYC, suspicious transaction reporting and secrecy duties at the counter
Map everyday banking situations to the right regulator and rule

runningCase.name: Liya's Who regulates what? board at Bank A
runningCase.text: Liya Bekele has just joined the Hawassa branch of Bank A, a fictional private Ethiopian bank, as a customer service officer. Her branch manager, W/ro Tigist Haile, gives her a board with two columns, Regulator and Rule, and 20 cards describing real kinds of branch situations: opening a diaspora account, a telebirr wallet, an IPO on ESX, a loan to a director's company and more. Each module adds cards and the rules behind them, using Bank A's illustrative figures (total capital of Birr 7,100 million and a Birr 60,000 million loan book), and Module 5 completes the board as the capstone.

modules.title: The Ethiopian financial system
modules.summary: See how Ethiopian banking grew from a state monopoly to a market open to private and foreign banks, and which institutions sit around the banks today.
objectives: Trace the main stages of Ethiopian banking from the 1974 nationalisation to the 2024 opening to foreign banks
Distinguish state, private, interest-free and foreign-owned banks
Name the non-bank institutions in the sector and who supervises each
Explain the roles of the NBE, ECMA, the Financial Intelligence Service and the deposit insurance fund

lessons.title: From nationalisation to an open market
body: Modern Ethiopian banking has gone through three big shifts. In 1974 the private banks and insurers were nationalised, and for twenty years the state owned the whole system. In 1994 the law reopened banking to private Ethiopian investors, and the private banks that dominate branch networks today grew from that reform.

For the next thirty years, banking stayed closed to foreign banks. The National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 591/2008 and the Banking Business Proclamation No. 592/2008, amended by Proclamation No. 1159/2019, were the base laws. In 2024 and 2025 both were replaced: the new Banking Business Proclamation, passed on 17 December 2024, opened the sector to foreign banks, and the new NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025 came into force on 4 February 2025.
Knowing this history helps you read the rules. Many directives still in force were issued under the 2008 laws, and the new proclamations keep them alive unless they conflict with the new text.

items.text: Private banks and insurers nationalised; the state runs the system.
Banking reopened to private Ethiopian investors.
NBE Proclamation No. 591/2008 and Banking Business Proclamation No. 592/2008.
Banking Business Proclamation amended by No. 1159/2019.
New Banking Business Proclamation passed (17 December): foreign banks may enter.
NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025 in force (4 February); revised licensing, recovery and capital directives follow.

example.title: Three generations at one branch
example.text: Ato Getachew Alemu joined a state bank in Dessie in 1986, when there was one bank to choose from. His daughter Meron joined a private bank in 2008 and watched dozens of competitors open branches in the same town. In 2026 his grandson Dawit, a new graduate, is preparing for interviews with a foreign bank subsidiary. Each of them worked under a different set of laws, and Dawit's first training is about the 2024 to 2025 reforms.

lessons.tip: When you meet a directive, check which proclamation it was issued under and whether a newer directive has repealed it.

lessons.title: The types of bank in Ethiopia today
body: Ethiopian banks now come in several forms. State-owned banks are owned by the government. Private domestic banks are share companies owned by Ethiopian shareholders, with limited room for foreign shareholders under the new rules. Interest-free banking is offered either through a window inside a conventional bank or by a full-fledged interest-free bank.

Since the 2024 reform a foreign bank can also enter, as a locally incorporated subsidiary, as a branch of the foreign parent, or by buying shares in a domestic bank. A foreign bank may also open a representative office, which is a liaison presence rather than a full bank. Each form has its own licence and capital rule, which Module 3 covers.

items.label: State-owned bank
items.text: Owned by the government; same prudential rules.

items.label: Private domestic bank
items.text: A share company owned mainly by Ethiopians.

items.label: Interest-free window or bank
items.text: Sharia-compliant products under SBB/72/2019.

items.label: Foreign subsidiary
items.text: An Ethiopian company owned by a foreign bank.

items.label: Foreign branch
items.text: Part of the foreign parent, with its own branch capital.

items.label: Representative office
items.text: A liaison office; USD 100,000 remitted in under SBB/94/2025.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/72/2019, interest-free banking
regulation.text: The directive, issued under Article 22(2) of Proclamation No. 592/2008, sets the rules for interest-free banking windows inside conventional banks and for full-fledged interest-free banks. A window must keep its interest-free business and funds apart from the conventional business.

scenario.title: Is the window a separate bank?
scenario.situation: Ustaz Kedir Mohammed wants to open a wadiah account at the interest-free window of Bank A's Jimma branch. He asks Liya, the new customer service officer, whether his money will be mixed with the bank's interest-earning loans and which rules protect him.
scenario.question: What is the best answer?
options: The window is a separate bank with its own NBE licence and capital
The window is part of Bank A, but SBB/72/2019 requires its interest-free business to be run apart from the conventional business
There is no specific rule; it is a marketing label
Only the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority supervises interest-free products
scenario.explain: A window sits inside a licensed conventional bank, and SBB/72/2019 sets how it must be kept apart. A full-fledged interest-free bank is a separate licensed bank. ECMA does not supervise bank deposits.

lessons.title: Beyond banks: the wider financial sector
body: Banks hold most of the sector's assets, but they share the market with other licensed institutions. Microfinance institutions serve small borrowers and savers. Insurers sell life and general cover. Payment instrument issuers run mobile wallets such as telebirr. Capital market service providers, such as brokers, dealers and investment advisers, serve investors on the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX), which opened in January 2025.

The NBE supervises more than banks: it also licenses and supervises insurers, microfinance institutions and payment instrument issuers. Capital market firms and the exchange fall under the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority (ECMA), set up under the Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021.
points: Payment instrument issuers and payment system operators: NBE, under the National Payment System law
Securities exchange, brokers, dealers, investment banks, advisers: ECMA
ECMA Directive No. 980/2024 sets 15 licence categories for capital market service providers

example.title: One trader, five regulated institutions
example.text: W/ro Almaz Bekele sells coffee in Hawassa. She keeps her business account at a bank, repays a working capital loan to a microfinance institution, insures her pickup with an insurer, takes customer payments on telebirr and has just bought shares through a broker on ESX. The first four are supervised by the NBE; the broker and the exchange are supervised by ECMA.

lessons.title: Who regulates what: four public bodies
body: Four public bodies matter most to a bank employee. The NBE licenses and supervises banks and sets their prudential rules. ECMA regulates the capital market, including any bank that issues shares to the public or owns a capital market subsidiary. The Financial Intelligence Service receives suspicious transaction reports and leads the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing under the AML/CFT law.

The deposit insurance fund protects depositors up to a set amount if a member bank fails, which reduces the risk of panic withdrawals. The coverage limit can change, so always check the current figure before quoting it to a customer.

left.title: NBE and ECMA (rule makers and supervisors)
items: NBE: licensing, prudential directives, inspection, resolution of banks
NBE: also insurers, microfinance institutions, payment issuers
ECMA: securities exchange, public offers, capital market firms

right.title: FIS and deposit insurance (specialist bodies)
items: Financial Intelligence Service: receives suspicious transaction reports
FIS: AML/CFT guidance for banks and other reporting entities
Deposit insurance fund: pays insured depositors if a member bank fails

scenario.title: A complaint about a broker
scenario.situation: Ato Tesfaye Gebre walks into a Bank A branch upset. A licensed broker in Addis Ababa placed an ESX order for him at a price he did not authorise. He asks the branch to report the broker to the NBE.
scenario.question: Where should Liya point him?
options: The NBE, because it supervises all financial firms
The Ethiopian Capital Market Authority, which licenses and supervises brokers
scenario.explain: Brokers are capital market service providers licensed by ECMA. The NBE supervises banks, insurers, MFIs and payment issuers; the FIS handles suspicious transactions; the deposit insurance fund protects bank deposits.

lessons.title: Why banks are regulated so closely
body: A bank lends money that belongs to its depositors. Most of its balance sheet is funded by deposits and only a small part by the owners' capital. That leverage means a modest loss on loans can wipe out a large share of capital, and depositors would bear the rest if no rules stood in the way.

Banks are also linked to each other and to the payment system. If one bank fails, depositors at others may panic and the payment chain can break. Prudential rules on capital, liquidity, concentration and provisioning exist to keep each bank strong enough to absorb losses before they reach depositors.

worked.title: Bank A: how leverage magnifies a loan loss (Birr millions, illustrative)
worked.note: A loss of 5% of total assets (4,000 of 120,000) removes a third of the bank's capital. This is why the NBE sets minimum capital ratios and limits on concentration.

lessons.tip: When a rule feels like paperwork, ask which depositor it protects.

lessons.title: The running case: Liya's mapping board
body: Throughout this course you follow Liya Bekele, a new customer service officer at the Hawassa branch of Bank A, a fictional private Ethiopian bank. Her branch manager, W/ro Tigist Haile, gives her a board with two columns, Regulator and Rule, and a stack of 20 cards, each describing a real kind of situation from branch life.

In each module Liya sorts a few more cards. By the end of Module 5 she has placed all 20 and can explain each one to a customer. Her first card reads: a customer living in Washington wants to open a diaspora foreign currency account.

scenario.title: Card 1: the diaspora account
scenario.situation: Ato Henok Tadesse, an Ethiopian living in Washington, wants to open a foreign currency account at Bank A through his sister in Hawassa and send dollars monthly. Liya must place this card on the board.
scenario.question: Which regulator and rules belong on the card?
options: ECMA, under the Capital Market Proclamation
The NBE, under the Foreign Exchange Directive No. FXD/01/2024 and the KYC/CDD rules
No regulator; foreign currency accounts are a bank's own product
scenario.explain: Foreign currency accounts for non-residents are governed by the NBE's FXD/01/2024, and the bank must identify the customer under its KYC/CDD rules. The FIS would only come in if something suspicious appeared.

example.title: Why the manager uses a board
example.text: W/ro Tigist noticed that new staff could quote product features but froze when a customer asked who to complain to or why a document was needed. Sorting real cases by regulator and rule gave her team a mental map they could use at the counter, and complaints sent to the wrong office fell within a quarter.

takeaways: Ethiopian banking moved from a state monopoly (1974) to private Ethiopian banks (1994) and opened to foreign banks with the new Banking Business Proclamation (December 2024).
NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025 has been in force since 4 February 2025; many older directives remain in force unless they conflict with it.
Banks take several forms: state, private, interest-free window or bank, foreign subsidiary and foreign branch.
The NBE supervises banks, insurers, microfinance institutions and payment issuers; ECMA supervises the capital market; the FIS receives suspicious transaction reports.
Leverage is why banks are regulated: a small loss on assets can remove a large share of capital.

quiz.q: In which year were private banks and insurers nationalised in Ethiopia?
quiz.explain: The 1974 nationalisation brought the whole system under state ownership until the 1994 reopening.

quiz.q: Which body supervises insurance companies in Ethiopia?
quiz.explain: The NBE supervises insurers and microfinance institutions as well as banks.

quiz.q: A broker on the Ethiopian Securities Exchange is licensed by:
quiz.explain: Brokers are capital market service providers under ECMA.

quiz.q: Which directive governs interest-free banking windows?
quiz.explain: SBB/72/2019 covers interest-free windows and full-fledged interest-free banks.

quiz.q: A bank funded 90% by deposits loses 5% of its assets. Why is this serious?
options: The loss falls first on a thin layer of capital, which may be largely wiped out
quiz.explain: With capital of about 10% of assets, a 5% loss removes about half of it.

quiz.q: Where should a bank report a suspicious transaction?
quiz.explain: The FIS receives suspicious transaction reports under the AML/CFT law.

modules.title: The NBE and its mandate
modules.summary: Understand what NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025 asks the central bank to do, how it is governed, and how its directives reach every branch.
objectives: State the NBE's objectives in their legal order of priority
Describe the NBE Board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the Financial Stability Committee
Explain the limits on NBE lending to government
Recognise the NBE powers that affect customers directly, such as consumer protection and the crypto payment ban
Read a directive number and tell which area it covers

lessons.title: A new charter: Proclamation No. 1359/2025
body: The National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025 came into force on 4 February 2025, published in Negarit Gazette No. 14. It replaces Proclamation No. 591/2008 and gives the NBE a modern central bank charter: it is autonomous in carrying out its duties and accountable to the Prime Minister.

The proclamation keeps continuity. Under Article 55, directives issued before it stay in force unless they are inconsistent with the new law. That is why a bank in 2026 still applies directives issued in 2019 or 2024 alongside the newer 2025 directives.

regulation.source: National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Article 55
regulation.text: Directives issued by the NBE before the proclamation remain applicable unless they are inconsistent with it. Staff should therefore check both whether a directive has been repealed by a newer one and whether it conflicts with the 2025 proclamation.

example.title: An old directive still in use
example.text: In a staff meeting at Bank A's Adama branch, Ato Yonas Bekele asked why the bank still cites SBB/72/2019 on interest-free banking when the base law changed in 2025. The compliance officer, W/ro Hiwot Mulugeta, explained that the new proclamation keeps earlier directives in force unless they conflict with it, and that no newer directive has repealed SBB/72/2019.

lessons.title: Objectives in order: price stability first
body: Article 5 of the proclamation ranks the NBE's objectives. Price stability comes first. Financial stability comes second. Supporting economic growth comes third, as long as it does not undermine the first two.

The order matters in practice. Since 2024 the NBE has run an interest-rate-based monetary policy framework built around the National Bank Rate. At its Monetary Policy Committee meeting No. 7 on 13 July 2026, it raised the National Bank Rate by 1 point to 16% as headline inflation had risen to 13.4% in May 2026, and it removed the temporary credit growth cap. Rates and settings change at each meeting, so always check the latest MPC release.

items.label: Price stability
items.text: The primary objective (Article 5).

items.label: Financial stability
items.text: A sound banking and payment system.

items.label: Economic growth
items.text: Supported without undermining the first two.

scenario.title: Why raise rates when businesses want credit?
scenario.situation: A hotel owner in Bahir Dar, W/ro Selamawit Ayele, tells Liya that the NBE should cut rates to help tourism, not raise them. Inflation was 13.4% in May 2026 and the NBE raised the National Bank Rate to 16% in July 2026.
scenario.question: Which explanation is most accurate?
options: The NBE raised rates to increase bank profits
The law makes price stability the NBE's primary objective, so it may tighten policy when inflation rises even if borrowers would prefer lower rates
The Prime Minister sets the National Bank Rate directly
Rates were raised because foreign banks asked for it
scenario.explain: Article 5 of Proclamation No. 1359/2025 puts price stability first. Growth is supported only within that priority. The NBE is autonomous in its duties and accountable to the Prime Minister, who does not set the rate.

lessons.title: The Board and its committees
body: The NBE is governed by a 9-member Board. Two committees carry its main policy work. The Monetary Policy Committee, with 7 members (Article 23), decides the policy rate and other monetary settings. The Financial Stability Committee, also with 7 members (Article 24), watches risks to the whole system and publishes an annual financial stability report.

For a bank employee, the MPC release is the document that most often changes daily work: it can move the policy rate, the reserve requirement or foreign exchange settings. In July 2026, for example, MPC No. 7 introduced a targeted reserve requirement that the NBE may impose on individual banks based on their loan-to-deposit ratio.

items.label: NBE Board
items.text: 9 members; governs the bank.

items.label: Monetary Policy Committee
items.text: 7 members; sets the National Bank Rate and monetary settings (Art. 23).

items.label: Financial Stability Committee
items.text: 7 members; annual financial stability report (Art. 24).

lessons.tip: Save each MPC press release; trainers and auditors will ask which settings applied on a given date.

lessons.title: Limits on lending to government
body: A central bank that lends freely to its government can fuel inflation. Article 27 of the proclamation therefore limits NBE credit to government. Any direct advance or overdraft must be repaid within at most 12 months, and the amount may not exceed 15% of the government's average revenue. The NBE also may not buy government securities in the primary market.

Government borrowing therefore goes mainly through the market, for example through Treasury bill auctions where banks and other investors bid. This is one reason why Treasury bill yields, such as the 11.0% 91-day yield reported in the July 2026 MPC release, matter to bank treasurers.

worked.title: Testing a government overdraft request against Article 27 (Birr billions, illustrative)
worked.note: The request breaks the 15% ceiling by Birr 25 billion. The NBE could advance at most Birr 135 billion, repayable within 12 months, and could not instead buy new Treasury bills directly from the government.

scenario.title: Primary or secondary market?
scenario.situation: A trainee at Bank A's treasury reads that the government will issue new 364-day Treasury bills next week. He assumes the NBE will buy most of the issue at the auction to keep yields low.
scenario.question: What does Proclamation No. 1359/2025 say?
options: The NBE may buy any amount at the auction
The NBE may not buy government securities in the primary market
The NBE must buy at least 15% of each issue
Only foreign banks may bid at auctions
scenario.explain: Article 27 bars NBE purchases of government securities in the primary market and caps direct advances at 15% of average revenue for at most 12 months.

lessons.title: Powers that touch every customer
body: Beyond monetary policy, the proclamation gives the NBE wide powers over the financial system. It licenses and supervises banks and other financial institutions, and can step in to resolve a failing bank. It acts as lender of last resort (Article 30). Foreign exchange may be dealt only through banks and authorised dealers (Article 39), and the NBE may freeze funds for up to 10 days (Article 50).

Some powers reach customers directly. Article 41 gives the NBE consumer protection duties. Article 37 bans the use of crypto assets for payments unless the NBE permits it. Article 48 allows the NBE to issue a central bank digital currency.
points: Art. 37: no crypto payments without NBE permission
Art. 39: foreign exchange only through banks and authorised dealers
Art. 48: power to issue a central bank digital currency
Art. 50: fund freezing for up to 10 days

scenario.title: Paying a supplier in crypto
scenario.situation: Ato Biniam Tesfaye, who imports phone accessories, asks Bank A to help him pay a Dubai supplier in a cryptocurrency because it is faster than a letter of credit.
scenario.question: How should the bank respond?
options: Process it; crypto is not regulated in Ethiopia
Decline: crypto payments are banned unless the NBE permits them, and foreign exchange must go through banks and authorised dealers
Send him to ECMA for a crypto licence
Allow it if the amount is below Birr 1 million
scenario.explain: Article 37 bans crypto payments without NBE permission, and Article 39 channels foreign exchange through banks and authorised dealers. The bank should offer a lawful payment mode under FXD/01/2024.

example.title: A frozen account explained
example.text: A customer in Mekelle, W/ro Rahel Gebremedhin, found that a business account she was due to receive money from had been frozen on NBE instruction. Her relationship officer explained that the NBE can order a freeze for up to 10 days while a matter is examined, and that the bank must follow the order and cannot discuss its details.

lessons.title: How directives are issued and numbered
body: Proclamations are passed by Parliament. The NBE then issues directives that set the detailed rules. Each directive carries a series code, a running number and the year, for example SBB/90/2024. The code tells you the area: SBB for banking business licensing and supervision, FXD for foreign exchange, ONPS for the national payment system, FCP for financial consumer protection, INT for interest rates and MFI for microfinance.

A new directive usually states which older directive it repeals. SBB/90/2024 on asset classification and provisioning, for example, repealed SBB/69/2018. Before you rely on a directive, check that it is still in force and whether it has been amended.

items.label: SBB
items.text: Licensing and supervision of banking business.

items.label: FXD
items.text: Foreign exchange, e.g. FXD/01/2024.

items.label: ONPS
items.text: National payment system, e.g. ONPS/09/2023.

items.label: FCP
items.text: Financial consumer protection, e.g. FCP/01/2020.

items.label: INT
items.text: Interest rates, e.g. NBE/INT/13/2026.

items.label: MFI
items.text: Microfinance institutions.

worked.title: Decoding a directive number

rows.label: Series
rows.value: SBB: banking business licensing and supervision

worked.note: Any lesson, policy or memo that still cites SBB/69/2018 is out of date.

example.title: Liya decodes three cards
example.text: Liya picks three cards: an exporter asking about retaining dollars, a customer comparing savings rates, and a mobile wallet limit. Using the series codes she writes FXD/01/2024 on the first, NBE/INT/13/2026 on the second and ONPS on the third, then checks the NBE website for amendments, finding that FXD/01/2024 has been amended several times since 2024.

takeaways: NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025 has applied since 4 February 2025 and keeps earlier directives in force unless inconsistent (Art. 55).
Price stability is the NBE's primary objective, followed by financial stability and then growth (Art. 5).
A 9-member Board governs the NBE; the 7-member MPC and 7-member FSC carry monetary and stability policy.
NBE advances to government are capped at 15% of average revenue for at most 12 months, with no primary-market purchases (Art. 27).
Crypto payments are banned without NBE permission (Art. 37); consumer protection is an NBE duty (Art. 41).
Directive codes such as SBB, FXD, ONPS, FCP and INT show the area a rule covers.

quiz.q: What is the NBE's primary objective under Proclamation No. 1359/2025?
quiz.explain: Article 5 ranks price stability first, then financial stability, then growth.

quiz.q: How many members sit on the NBE Monetary Policy Committee?
quiz.explain: The MPC has 7 members (Art. 23); the Board has 9.

quiz.q: A direct NBE overdraft to government may not exceed:
options: 5% of average revenue, repayable in 6 months
15% of average revenue, repayable within 12 months
quiz.explain: Article 27 sets the 15% and 12-month limits.

quiz.q: A directive numbered FXD/04/2026 most likely covers:
quiz.explain: FXD is the foreign exchange series.

quiz.q: Can an earlier directive still apply after 4 February 2025?
options: Yes, unless it is inconsistent with the new proclamation or repealed by a newer directive
quiz.explain: Article 55 keeps earlier directives in force unless inconsistent.

quiz.q: Which article allows the NBE to issue a central bank digital currency?
quiz.explain: Article 48 gives the CBDC power; Article 37 is the crypto payment ban.

modules.title: Licensing and ownership
modules.summary: Learn who may own and run an Ethiopian bank, how foreign banks can enter, and what capital a bank needs to obtain and keep its licence.
objectives: Describe what the Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025 changed
State the capital and renewal rules of SBB/94/2025 for new banks, foreign subsidiaries and branches
Compare the foreign entry modes and apply the foreign shareholding caps
Explain fit and proper approval for persons with significant influence under SBB/89/2024

lessons.title: The Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025
body: The new Banking Business Proclamation was passed on 17 December 2024 and repeals Proclamation No. 592/2008 as amended by No. 1159/2019. NBE directives issued in 2025, such as SBB/93/2025 on recovery plans and SBB/95/2025 on capital adequacy, cite it as Proclamation No. 1360/2025. It governs who may carry on banking business, ownership, foreign bank entry and the NBE's prudential powers.

Its biggest change is opening Ethiopian banking to foreign banks. A foreign bank may set up a subsidiary, open a branch or buy shares in an existing domestic bank. The directives issued in June 2024, SBB/87 to SBB/92, were made under the old Proclamation No. 592/2008 and continue to apply.

regulation.source: Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025 (citation as confirmed by SBB/93/2025)
regulation.text: No person may carry on banking business in Ethiopia without an NBE licence. The proclamation provides for foreign participation through a subsidiary, a branch or the acquisition of shares in a domestic bank, and empowers the NBE to issue prudential directives. The official gazette text was still being confirmed when this course was written, so rely on the directives for detailed figures.

example.title: A question from a shareholder
example.text: At Bank A's annual meeting in Addis Ababa, shareholder Ato Mesfin Haile asked whether foreign banks would now take over the market. The chief executive explained that the 2024 law lets foreign banks enter in three ways but keeps every one of them under the same NBE licensing, capital and prudential rules as Ethiopian banks.

lessons.title: Getting and keeping a licence: SBB/94/2025
body: Directive No. SBB/94/2025, in force since 25 June 2025, sets the licensing path. A new domestic bank and a foreign bank subsidiary each need at least Birr 5 billion of paid-up capital, and a foreign bank branch needs Birr 5 billion of branch capital. Foreign banks pay their capital in acceptable foreign currency. A representative office needs at least USD 100,000 remitted into Ethiopia.

A licence is not permanent: banks renew it every year, applying between 1 July and 30 September. The directive also sets licensing and renewal fees and repeals the older licensing directive, SBB/56/2013.

items.label: Apply to the NBE
items.text: Business plan, shareholders, proposed directors and managers.

items.label: Fit and proper review
items.text: Influential shareholders, directors and executives under SBB/89/2024.

items.label: Pay up capital
items.text: Birr 5 billion; in foreign currency for foreign banks.

items.label: Receive the licence
items.text: Start banking business under NBE supervision.

items.label: Renew every year
items.text: Application between 1 July and 30 September.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/94/2025, licensing and renewal of banking business
regulation.text: Minimum paid-up capital of Birr 5 billion for a new domestic bank or a foreign bank subsidiary, and Birr 5 billion of branch capital for a foreign bank branch; at least USD 100,000 for a representative office. Licences are renewed annually. In force 25 June 2025; repeals SBB/56/2013.

lessons.title: Foreign bank entry and foreign shareholding caps
body: A subsidiary is an Ethiopian company owned by the foreign bank, with its own board and capital. A branch is part of the foreign parent, with branch capital held in Ethiopia. A foreign investor can also buy shares in a domestic bank, within limits.

SBB/94/2025 caps foreign ownership of a domestic bank. Foreign nationals and foreign-owned Ethiopian organisations together may hold up to 49%. Direct caps are 7% for a foreign individual, 10% for a foreign company and 40% for a strategic investor. A separate NBE draft directive on foreign equity investment (October 2025) proposes the same caps and payment in US dollars, euros or pounds sterling; check whether a final version has been issued.

left.title: Foreign subsidiary
items: Birr 5 billion paid-up capital in foreign currency

right.title: Foreign branch
items: Part of the foreign parent bank
Birr 5 billion branch capital in foreign currency
Same NBE prudential rules apply locally

worked.title: Bank A: room for a foreign strategic investor (subscribed capital Birr 6,000 million)
worked.note: The binding limit is the 49% aggregate cap, not the 40% strategic cap. Any holding of 2% or more also needs NBE approval as an influential shareholder.

lessons.title: Minimum capital for existing banks
body: Existing banks face their own capital floor. Directive SBB/78/2021 is reported to require a minimum paid-up capital of ETB 5 billion, to be reached by 30 June 2026. Erudite had not received the official text of SBB/78/2021 when this course was written, so treat these figures as reported and check the NBE's current position.

A bank short of the minimum can raise capital from shareholders, retain profits instead of paying dividends, or merge with another bank. Questions on bank mergers after the June 2026 deadline should go to your compliance team, which follows NBE guidance as it is issued.

scenario.title: A capital gap before the deadline
scenario.situation: In early 2026 a small private bank had paid-up capital of Birr 3.6 billion against the reported ETB 5 billion floor. Its board debated three options: a rights issue to shareholders, skipping the dividend, or merging with a bank of similar size.
scenario.question: What was the size of the gap, and which statement is right?
options: Birr 1.4 billion; any of the three routes can close it if the NBE approves the shareholders and any merger
Birr 0.4 billion; only a merger is allowed
There is no gap because deposits count as capital
Birr 5 billion; the bank must close
scenario.explain: 5.0 minus 3.6 is Birr 1.4 billion. Capital can come from new shares, retained earnings or a merger, each subject to NBE approvals. Deposits are liabilities, not capital.

example.title: A rights issue at a regional bank
example.text: A fictional regional bank, Bank C, offered existing shareholders one new share for every two held. Ato Abebe Kassa, a teacher in Debre Markos with 40 shares, could buy 20 more. Shareholders who did not take up their rights saw their percentage fall, and anyone whose holding rose to 2% or more needed NBE approval.

lessons.title: Who may own and run a bank: fit and proper
body: Under Directive SBB/89/2024, persons with significant influence need NBE approval. They are influential shareholders, meaning those holding 2% or more of subscribed capital, directors, the chief executive officer and senior executive officers. The NBE checks integrity, financial soundness and competence before approval. SBB/89/2024 repealed SBB/79/2021.

Board structure is set by SBB/91/2024 on corporate governance: at least 9 directors, one-third independent, at least 2 women, and a 6-year limit on consecutive service. The board must have four committees: audit, risk management and compliance, nomination and remuneration, and credit. The chief risk officer needs NBE approval before appointment.

items.label: Influential shareholders
items.text: 2% or more of subscribed capital: NBE approval.

items.label: Directors
items.text: At least 9; one-third independent; at least 2 women.

items.label: CEO and senior executives
items.text: NBE approval under SBB/89/2024.

items.label: Chief risk officer
items.text: NBE prior approval under SBB/91/2024.

scenario.title: Card 9: a 3% shareholder
scenario.situation: Dr. Sara Wolde, an Ethiopian surgeon, plans to buy shares in Bank A that would bring her holding to 3% of subscribed capital. Her broker says she can just sign the transfer form at the share department.
scenario.question: What must happen first?
options: Nothing; only foreign investors need approval
The NBE must approve her as an influential shareholder because the holding is 2% or more
She must first join the board
scenario.explain: SBB/89/2024 requires NBE approval for shareholders reaching 2% or more of subscribed capital, whether Ethiopian or foreign.

lessons.title: Special licences: zone branches and interest-free banks
body: Some activities need a specific licence on top of the banking licence. Under SBB/99/2026, in force since 6 January 2026, a bank needs a branch licence before operating in a Special Economic Zone. The tests include at least 1% of banking sector assets (waived for new foreign banks in their first two years) and a capital adequacy ratio two points above the minimum. Zone branches must offer foreign exchange services and serve only zone residents.
Interest-free banking follows SBB/72/2019, which provides both for windows in conventional banks and for full-fledged interest-free banks.

example.title: A zone branch application
example.text: Bank A wants a branch in an industrial park that has become a Special Economic Zone. Its total capital ratio is 11.1%, against an 11% minimum. The planning team, led by Ato Kalkidan Assefa, realises that SBB/99/2026 needs a ratio two points above the minimum, about 13%, so the bank must build capital before it can apply.

lessons.tip: Before promising a customer a new service or location, ask whether it needs its own NBE licence.

takeaways: The Banking Business Proclamation (cited as No. 1360/2025) repealed No. 592/2008 and opened banking to foreign banks.
SBB/94/2025 sets Birr 5 billion paid-up or branch capital for new banks, foreign subsidiaries and branches, USD 100,000 for representative offices, and annual renewal between 1 July and 30 September.
Foreign ownership of a domestic bank is capped at 49% in aggregate, with 7%, 10% and 40% direct caps for individuals, companies and strategic investors.
SBB/78/2021 is reported to require ETB 5 billion paid-up capital for existing banks by 30 June 2026.
Holdings of 2% or more, directors, the CEO and senior executives need NBE approval under SBB/89/2024.

quiz.q: What paid-up capital does SBB/94/2025 require for a new foreign bank subsidiary?
quiz.explain: Birr 5 billion applies to new domestic banks, foreign subsidiaries and, as branch capital, foreign branches.

quiz.q: When do banks apply for annual licence renewal under SBB/94/2025?
quiz.explain: Renewal runs between 1 July and 30 September each year.

quiz.q: What is the aggregate cap on foreign ownership of a domestic bank?
quiz.explain: Foreign holders together may own up to 49%; 40% is the strategic investor cap.

quiz.q: Foreign investors already hold 35% of a domestic bank. What is the largest new stake a strategic investor could take?
quiz.explain: The 49% aggregate cap leaves 14%, which is below the 40% strategic cap.

quiz.q: Which holding makes a shareholder influential under SBB/89/2024?
quiz.explain: Influential shareholders hold 2% or more of subscribed capital.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four mandatory board committees under SBB/91/2024?
quiz.explain: The four are audit, risk management and compliance, nomination and remuneration, and credit.

modules.title: Prudential rules in plain language
modules.summary: Understand what the NBE's capital, liquidity, concentration, investment and provisioning rules require and why each one protects depositors.
objectives: Explain the three capital ratios of SBB/95/2025 and compute a simple capital ratio
Describe why liquidity rules and the loan-to-deposit ratio matter
Apply the large exposure and related-party limits to simple figures
State the SBB/92/2024 investment limits
Classify a loan by days past due and compute minimum provisions under SBB/90/2024

lessons.title: Capital adequacy: SBB/95/2025
body: Capital is the owners' money that absorbs losses before depositors are hurt. Directive SBB/95/2025 moves Ethiopian banks to risk-based capital. Banks must hold Common Equity Tier 1 (mainly paid-up shares and retained earnings) of at least 7% of risk-weighted assets, Tier 1 of at least 9% and total capital of at least 11%.

Risk-weighted assets give each asset a weight by its risk: for example 0% for Birr exposures to the Ethiopian government, 35% for qualifying residential mortgages and 100% for unrated corporate loans. Charges for market risk and operational risk are added. The directive came into force on 10 November 2025, with quarterly reports from the first quarter of 2026 and full compliance by 31 December 2026. It repeals the old capital directive SBB/9/95.

visual.caption: Minimums: CET1 7%, Tier 1 9%, total capital 11% of risk-weighted assets.

worked.title: Bank A: capital ratios under SBB/95/2025 (Birr millions, illustrative)

rows.label: Birr Treasury bills and government bonds: 25,000 x 0%

worked.note: Bank A passes all three tests, but only just. A Birr 1,000 million rise in corporate loans would push total capital to 10.9% of RWA, below the minimum.

example.title: Why the loan pipeline paused
example.text: In late 2026 Bank A's credit team in Dire Dawa was told to slow new corporate lending for a month. Branch staff were puzzled, as deposits were growing. The reason was capital: every Birr 100 of unrated corporate loans adds Birr 100 of risk-weighted assets and needs about Birr 11 of capital, and the bank's total ratio was close to 11%.

lessons.title: Liquidity: cash to meet withdrawals
body: A bank can be solvent and still fail if it cannot pay depositors on the day they ask. The NBE therefore requires banks to hold a minimum share of liquid assets, such as cash, balances at the NBE and Treasury bills, against their liabilities. Check the current liquidity directive for the exact ratio, as Erudite is still confirming the latest text.

The loan-to-deposit ratio shows how much of its deposits a bank has lent out. The July 2026 MPC release reported a private-bank loan-to-deposit ratio of 72.7% and introduced a targeted reserve requirement that the NBE may impose on individual banks according to their loan-to-deposit ratio. At the same meeting it removed the temporary credit growth cap.

scenario.title: A rumour at the branch
scenario.situation: A false social media rumour says Bank A is in trouble. By noon, customers at the Hawassa branch have withdrawn three times the normal daily amount. Liya's manager asks why the bank can keep paying without selling loans.
scenario.question: What lets the bank keep paying?
options: Its liquid assets: cash, balances at the NBE and Treasury bills it can sell or use
Its loan book, which customers repay on demand
Its fixed assets such as branch buildings
Its annual profit, paid out daily
scenario.explain: Liquidity rules make banks hold assets that can be turned into cash quickly. Loans and buildings cannot pay depositors on the same day, and the NBE can also act as lender of last resort.

lessons.title: Large exposures: SBB/87/2024
body: If a bank lends too much to one group, that group's failure can sink the bank. Directive SBB/87/2024 defines a large exposure as one of 10% or more of total capital and caps exposure to any single counterparty group at 25% of total capital. Companies with common owners or control count as one group.

Some exposures are exempt, including the federal and state governments and their enterprises, government-guaranteed portions, the NBE and intraday interbank exposures. Banks report large exposures monthly, within 20 days of month-end.

worked.title: Bank A: the Tana Agro group (total capital Birr 7,100 million)
worked.note: Each company alone is within the limit, but the group is not. The bank must report the breach and bring the group below Birr 1,775 million.

scenario.title: Is a public enterprise loan a breach?
scenario.situation: Bank A has lent Birr 2,100 million, about 30% of its total capital, to a federal public enterprise building rural roads. A colleague says this is a large exposure breach.
scenario.question: Is she right?
options: Yes, any exposure above 25% is a breach
No, exposures to federal and state governments and their enterprises are exempt from the limit under SBB/87/2024
Yes, unless the loan is in foreign currency
scenario.explain: SBB/87/2024 exempts federal and state governments and their enterprises, government-guaranteed portions, the NBE and intraday interbank exposures from the 25% limit.

lessons.title: Related parties: SBB/88/2024
body: Related parties are people and companies close to the bank, such as shareholders with 2% or more, directors and senior managers, and the businesses linked to them. Loans to them can be granted on easy terms that ordinary customers would never get. Directive SBB/88/2024 limits exposure to 15% of total capital per related party and 35% for all related parties together.

Every related-party transaction must be on arm's-length terms, the same as for an unrelated customer. A transaction above Birr 15 million needs board approval after an opinion from the Audit Committee.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/88/2024, related party transactions
regulation.text: Exposure to a single related party may not exceed 15% of total capital, and to all related parties together 35%. Terms must be at arm's length. Transactions above Birr 15 million require board approval following an Audit Committee opinion. SBB/87/2024 and SBB/88/2024 together repealed SBB/53/2012.

scenario.title: Card 4: a loan to a director's company
scenario.situation: Ato Daniel Mekonnen, a director of Bank A, owns Metehara Cement PLC. The company asks for a Birr 40 million working capital loan at 2 points below the rate offered to similar customers. Bank A's total capital is Birr 7,100 million.
scenario.question: What is the correct treatment?
options: Approve at branch level; the amount is small relative to capital
Price it on the same terms as an unrelated borrower and send it to the board for approval after an Audit Committee opinion
Decline it; banks may never lend to directors' companies
Approve the discount because directors are low risk
scenario.explain: The loan is well within 15% of capital (Birr 1,065 million), but it exceeds Birr 15 million, so it needs board approval after an Audit Committee opinion, and the discount breaks the arm's-length rule.

lessons.title: Investment limits: SBB/92/2024
body: Banks are meant to lend, not to run other businesses. Directive SBB/92/2024, in force since 19 July 2024, limits their equity investments: 5% in a single insurer, 10% in any other single non-bank business, 15% of total capital for all non-bank equity investments together, and 10% of total capital in real estate. With NBE approval a bank may own up to 100% of a capital market service provider, such as an investment bank subsidiary.
The directive repealed SBB/65/2017. Check the directive for the base of each limit before you test a specific investment.

visual.caption: SBB/92/2024 limits; a capital market subsidiary may be owned up to 100% with NBE approval.

example.title: The insurer stake that was cut back
example.text: Bank A's strategy team, led by W/ro Bethlehem Girma, proposed buying 8% of a growing insurer to sell its policies in branches. Compliance pointed out that SBB/92/2024 allows only 5% in a single insurer. The bank bought 5% and signed a distribution agreement instead of buying more shares.

lessons.title: Loan classification and provisioning: SBB/90/2024
body: Directive SBB/90/2024 makes banks classify every loan by how far it is past due and set aside minimum provisions. Pass loans carry 1%, special mention (30 to 89 days past due) 3%, substandard (90 to 179 days) 20%, doubtful (180 to 359 days) 50% and loss (360 days or more) 100%. Collateral does not change the classification.

Loans in the substandard, doubtful and loss classes are non-performing, and interest on them stops being recognised as income. If 20% or more of a customer's exposure is non-performing, all of that customer's loans are reclassified. If the provision under IFRS is lower than the directive's minimum, the difference goes to a regulatory reserve.

worked.title: Bank A: minimum provisions on a Birr 60,000 million loan book
worked.note: The bank must move Birr 168 million to a regulatory reserve so that its cover reaches the SBB/90/2024 minimum.

scenario.title: Card 11: 100 days late, well secured
scenario.situation: Gondar Leather Works PLC is 100 days past due on a Birr 12 million loan. Its relationship manager argues that the loan should stay as special mention because it is secured by a building valued at Birr 30 million.
scenario.question: How should the loan be classified and provisioned?
options: Pass, 1%, because the collateral covers it
Substandard, 20%, which is Birr 2.4 million; collateral does not change the class
scenario.explain: 90 to 179 days past due is substandard under SBB/90/2024 regardless of collateral. 20% of Birr 12 million is Birr 2.4 million, and interest stops accruing.

takeaways: SBB/95/2025 requires CET1 of 7%, Tier 1 of 9% and total capital of 11% of risk-weighted assets, with full compliance by 31 December 2026.
Liquidity rules keep cash and near-cash ready for withdrawals; the NBE may add a targeted reserve requirement linked to a bank's loan-to-deposit ratio.
A large exposure is 10% or more of total capital; one group may not exceed 25% (SBB/87/2024).
Related parties are limited to 15% each and 35% together, on arm's-length terms, with board approval above Birr 15 million (SBB/88/2024).
SBB/92/2024 caps investments in insurers, other non-bank businesses and real estate.
SBB/90/2024 sets classes by days past due and minimum provisions of 1%, 3%, 20%, 50% and 100%.

quiz.q: What is the minimum total capital ratio under SBB/95/2025?
quiz.explain: Total capital must be at least 11% of risk-weighted assets; 7% and 9% are CET1 and Tier 1.

quiz.q: Under SBB/95/2025, what risk weight applies to an unrated corporate loan?
quiz.explain: Unrated corporates carry 100%; Birr sovereign exposures 0% and qualifying mortgages 35%.

quiz.q: A bank's total capital is Birr 4,000 million. What is its single group limit?
quiz.explain: 25% of Birr 4,000 million is Birr 1,000 million.

quiz.q: Which exposure is exempt from the SBB/87/2024 limit?
options: A loan to a large private brewery
A loan to a state government enterprise
A loan to a director's company
An overnight placement with a foreign bank
quiz.explain: Federal and state governments and their enterprises are exempt; intraday, not overnight, interbank exposures are exempt.

quiz.q: A loan is 200 days past due. What minimum provision applies?
quiz.explain: 180 to 359 days is doubtful, provisioned at 50%.

quiz.q: Above what amount does a related-party transaction need board approval under SBB/88/2024?
quiz.explain: Above Birr 15 million, after an Audit Committee opinion.

modules.title: Conduct, integrity and the mapping capstone
modules.summary: Apply consumer protection, KYC, suspicious transaction reporting and secrecy rules at the counter, then complete the 20-card Who regulates what? board.
objectives: Explain the main duties of financial consumer protection under FCP/01/2020
Describe the steps of KYC and customer due diligence
Recognise when to file a suspicious transaction report with the Financial Intelligence Service
Apply bank secrecy to customer information requests
Map 20 everyday situations to the right regulator and rule

lessons.title: Treating customers fairly: FCP/01/2020
body: The NBE's financial consumer protection directive, FCP/01/2020 (as reported; the full text is still being confirmed), sets how banks must treat customers. Its core duties are fair treatment, clear disclosure of prices, including loan costs shown as an annual percentage rate (APR), a working complaints process, and care with customer data. Article 41 of Proclamation No. 1359/2025 now also gives the NBE consumer protection duties.

Since NBE/INT/13/2026 (9 January 2026), banks set deposit and lending rates freely, with board approval and reporting to the NBE. Free pricing makes clear disclosure more important: customers can only compare offers if banks show them the full cost.
points: Disclose all fees and the APR before the customer signs
Record and answer complaints within the bank's set time
Tell customers how to escalate to the NBE if unresolved

scenario.title: Card 5: the undisclosed fee
scenario.situation: W/ro Hanna Desta took a Birr 300,000 personal loan from Bank A. Two months later she found a Birr 6,000 processing fee she says nobody mentioned. She asks Liya whether she has any right to complain.
scenario.question: What should Liya do?
options: Tell her fees are the bank's business and cannot be questioned
Register her complaint, check whether the fee and APR were disclosed before signing, and explain how she can escalate to the NBE if not resolved
Refund the fee from Liya's own till without recording it
scenario.explain: Consumer protection rules require disclosure of costs and a complaints process. Recording the complaint lets the bank fix it and gives the customer a route to the NBE.

lessons.title: Know your customer and due diligence
body: Before opening an account or a loan, a bank must know who the customer is. The NBE's KYC/CDD directive (2021; confirm the current number with compliance) requires banks to identify the customer, verify the identity, understand the purpose of the relationship and keep monitoring it. Higher-risk customers get enhanced due diligence.
The Fayda national digital ID now makes electronic identity checks possible. KYC exists because a bank that does not know its customers can be used to move criminal money without noticing.

items.label: Identify
items.text: Name, ID, address, occupation; Fayda ID where available.

items.label: Verify
items.text: Check documents or the digital ID record.

items.label: Understand
items.text: Purpose of the account, source of funds, expected activity.

items.label: Assess risk
items.text: Low, medium or high; enhanced checks for high risk.

items.label: Monitor
items.text: Watch transactions against the expected pattern.

example.title: A diaspora account done right
example.text: For Ato Henok Tadesse's diaspora account (Card 1), Liya collected a copy of his passport and residence permit through his sister, verified them with the bank's checklist, recorded that he would send about USD 800 a month from his salary, and set the account as medium risk because it is opened remotely. Six months later, a USD 40,000 transfer from an unknown company triggered a review.

lessons.title: Suspicious transactions and the FIS
body: The AML/CFT Proclamation (reported as No. 780/2013) requires banks to report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Service. A transaction is suspicious when it does not fit what the bank knows about the customer or seems designed to avoid controls, such as cash split into small amounts.

Staff do not need proof of a crime; they need a reasonable suspicion, passed to the bank's compliance officer, who decides on the report. Under bank procedures the customer must not be told that a report is being considered.

scenario.title: Card 6: the split deposits
scenario.situation: Over five days, a customer who says he is a student deposits cash at three Bank A branches, each time just below the amount that triggers extra checks. The total is Birr 2.8 million. His account had been almost inactive for a year.
scenario.question: What should the teller who notices it do?
options: Nothing; each deposit is below the threshold
Ask the customer directly if he is laundering money
Report the pattern internally to the compliance officer, who decides on a suspicious transaction report to the FIS, without alerting the customer
Close the account immediately and tell the customer why
scenario.explain: Splitting deposits to avoid thresholds and activity that does not fit the profile are classic red flags. The internal report goes to compliance, which reports to the FIS, and the customer is not alerted.

lessons.title: Bank secrecy and customer data
body: Customers trust banks with private information. Bank staff owe a duty of secrecy: balances, transactions and personal data are disclosed only to the customer, a properly authorised representative, or authorities with legal power, such as a court, the NBE or the FIS.

Consumer protection rules and the personal data protection law add duties on collecting, storing and sharing customer data. Fraudsters often call branches pretending to be relatives or officials, so staff must verify identity and authority before saying anything.

scenario.title: Card 20: the caller and the balance
scenario.situation: A man calls the Hawassa branch, says he is the son of W/ro Aster Mengistu, a long-time customer in hospital, and asks for her balance so he can pay her medical bills.
scenario.question: What is the correct response?
options: Give the balance; it is an emergency
Give only the last four digits of the account
Decline to disclose; explain that the customer or a properly authorised representative with a valid power of attorney can obtain the information
Ask him to email his ID and then give the balance
scenario.explain: Secrecy applies to relatives too. Only the customer, an authorised representative or an authority with legal power may receive account information.

example.title: A court order handled properly
example.text: Bank A's Bahir Dar branch received a court order for statements of a company in a commercial dispute. The branch manager, Ato Fikru Alemayehu, sent it to the legal team, which confirmed it, and only the statements named in the order were released. The customer's other accounts stayed confidential.

lessons.title: Supervision, penalties and why compliance pays
body: The NBE supervises banks through reports, off-site analysis and on-site inspections. Directives set reporting deadlines, such as the monthly large exposure report within 20 days, and most of them provide penalties for breaches and for late or false reporting. Under SBB/93/2025 every bank must also keep a board-approved recovery plan.

Penalties can include fines, restrictions on business, removal of approval for directors or executives, and, in serious cases, resolution of the bank under Proclamation No. 1359/2025. For a bank employee, compliance is part of everyday work: following the procedure, recording the decision and escalating anything unusual.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/93/2025, recovery plans
regulation.text: All banks, including foreign subsidiaries and branches, must prepare a recovery plan approved by the board, with indicators, scenarios and recovery options. The first plan was due within 8 months, with annual updates. Issued under Proclamation No. 1360/2025; in force 13 May 2025.

lessons.title: Capstone: the completed Who regulates what? board
body: Liya has now placed all 20 cards. For each one she can say who regulates the situation and which rule applies, and she knows when to call compliance. Compare her board with your own answers.

Notice the pattern: the NBE covers most cards, because it supervises banks, insurers, microfinance institutions and payment issuers. ECMA appears for the capital market, the FIS for suspicious transactions, and secrecy is a duty every employee carries.

worked.title: Liya's completed board: situation and regulator or rule

rows.label: 2. Opening a telebirr wallet
rows.value: NBE: payment instrument issuer rules (ONPS series)

rows.label: 5. Complaint about an undisclosed fee
rows.value: NBE: FCP/01/2020 and Art. 41 of Proc. 1359/2025

rows.label: 6. Repeated cash deposits split into small amounts
rows.value: FIS: suspicious transaction report under the AML/CFT law

rows.label: 7. Bank plans an 8% stake in an insurer
13. Microfinance institution opens a branch
rows.value: NBE: microfinance law and MFI directives

rows.label: 16. Exporter asks how much FX to convert
rows.value: NBE: FXD/01/2024 as amended and MPC settings

rows.label: 18. Customer wants to pay in crypto
19. Firm applies for a broker licence
20. Caller asks for a relative's balance
rows.value: Bank secrecy duty and consumer data protection

worked.note: 16 cards go to the NBE, 2 to ECMA, 1 to the FIS, and 1 to the secrecy duty every employee owes.

scenario.title: A card that fits two places
scenario.situation: A private bank plans to sell new shares to the public and list them on ESX. A new investor would end up with 4% of the bank. Liya's colleague insists the card belongs only under ECMA.
scenario.question: Where does it belong?
options: Only ECMA, because it is a public offer
Only the NBE, because it is a bank
Both: ECMA for the public offer and listing, and the NBE for approving the 4% shareholder under SBB/89/2024
scenario.explain: Some situations involve two regulators. The public offer falls under ECMA, while the NBE approves anyone reaching 2% or more of a bank's shares.

lessons.title: Review and recap
body: You now have a map of Ethiopian banking regulation: the institutions, the two key proclamations, the licensing rules and the prudential and conduct directives. The details will keep changing, because Ethiopian regulation changed substantially between 2024 and 2026 and will continue to evolve.
Make a habit of checking the NBE directives page and the latest MPC release, and ask compliance before quoting any figure that may have changed.

items.label: Institutions
items.text: NBE, ECMA, FIS, deposit insurance fund.

items.label: Laws
items.text: Proc. No. 1359/2025 (NBE) and No. 1360/2025 (banking business).

items.label: Conduct
items.text: FCP/01/2020, KYC/CDD, AML/CFT, secrecy.

example.title: Liya at the counter, three months later
example.text: When a customer asked whether a new foreign bank in Addis Ababa was safer than Bank A, Liya explained that both are licensed by the NBE, both must meet the same capital rules of SBB/95/2025, and both are subject to the same inspections. The customer stayed, and Liya's manager added the question to the branch's training cards.

lessons.tip: Keep a one-page list of the directives you use most, with their in-force dates, and update it every quarter.

takeaways: FCP/01/2020 requires fair treatment, full disclosure including APR, complaint handling and data care.
KYC means identify, verify, understand, assess risk and monitor; the Fayda ID supports electronic checks.
Suspicion, not proof, triggers an internal report; compliance decides on a report to the FIS, and the customer is not alerted.
Account information goes only to the customer, an authorised representative or an authority with legal power.
Most situations map to the NBE; capital market matters go to ECMA, and some situations involve both.

quiz.q: How should loan costs be shown to customers under FCP/01/2020?
options: As a monthly flat fee only
As an annual percentage rate including fees
Only for loans above Birr 1 million
quiz.explain: APR disclosure lets customers compare the full cost of credit.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of KYC steps?
options: Identify, verify, understand, assess risk, monitor
Assess risk, open account, identify later
quiz.explain: Identity comes first, then verification, purpose, risk rating and ongoing monitoring.

quiz.q: Who receives suspicious transaction reports from banks?
quiz.explain: The FIS receives STRs under the AML/CFT law.

quiz.q: A teller suspects a customer's deposits are designed to avoid checks. What should she do first?
options: Report internally to the compliance officer
Ignore it unless she has proof
quiz.explain: Suspicion is enough; compliance decides on the FIS report.

quiz.q: Which request for account information may a bank lawfully answer?
quiz.explain: Courts and authorities with legal power may obtain information; others may not.

quiz.q: Under SBB/93/2025, who must approve a bank's recovery plan?
quiz.explain: Recovery plans need board approval.

exam.q: Which sequence correctly orders the main stages of Ethiopian banking?
options: Private banks reopened, nationalisation, foreign entry
Nationalisation (1974), private Ethiopian banks reopened (1994), foreign banks allowed (2024)
exam.explain: The state took over in 1974, private Ethiopian banks returned from 1994, and the December 2024 proclamation opened entry to foreign banks.

exam.q: A customer is unhappy with how a licensed microfinance institution handled her loan, and separately with a broker's ESX trade. Which pair of regulators is right?
options: FIS for the MFI, NBE for the broker
NBE for the MFI, ECMA for the broker
exam.explain: The NBE supervises MFIs; ECMA supervises brokers and the exchange.

exam.q: Bank A has assets of Birr 50,000 million and capital of Birr 5,000 million. Loans of Birr 4,000 million default with a 50% recovery. What share of capital is lost?
exam.explain: The loss is Birr 2,000 million, which is 40% of Birr 5,000 million of capital.

exam.q: A 2019 NBE directive has not been repealed by any newer directive. Does it still apply after 4 February 2025?
options: No, Proclamation No. 1359/2025 cancelled all earlier directives
Only if the bank's board adopts it again
Yes, unless it is inconsistent with Proclamation No. 1359/2025
exam.explain: Article 55 keeps earlier directives in force unless they are inconsistent with the new proclamation.

exam.q: The government asks the NBE for a 15-month overdraft equal to 10% of average revenue. Which part of Article 27 does it break?
exam.explain: 10% is within the 15% amount cap, but the overdraft must be repaid within at most 12 months.

exam.q: Inflation rises sharply while businesses ask for cheaper credit. Under Article 5, how should the NBE weigh these?
options: Price stability first, then financial stability, then growth
Growth first, as credit drives jobs
It must follow the borrowers' majority view
exam.explain: The law ranks price stability as the primary objective.

exam.q: Which directive would you open to check a mobile wallet's daily balance limit?
exam.explain: Payment instrument issuers, including mobile money, are governed by the ONPS series.

exam.q: A foreign bank wants to operate in Ethiopia as part of its parent company rather than as a separate Ethiopian company. What does it need?
options: A branch licence with Birr 5 billion branch capital in foreign currency
exam.explain: A foreign branch is part of the parent and needs Birr 5 billion branch capital under SBB/94/2025.

exam.q: Foreign investors hold 41% of a domestic bank. A foreign company wants 10%. What is the most it can buy?
exam.explain: The 49% aggregate cap leaves 8%, which is below the 10% company cap.

exam.q: A bank's licence was valid for the 2025/26 year. When must it apply for renewal?
exam.explain: SBB/94/2025 requires annual renewal applications between 1 July and 30 September.

exam.q: A new chief risk officer is selected by a bank's board. Which statement is right?
options: No approval is needed for risk staff
The NBE must approve the appointment in advance
exam.explain: SBB/91/2024 requires NBE prior approval of the CRO, and SBB/89/2024 covers senior executives.

exam.q: Risk-weighted assets are Birr 40,000 million and total capital is Birr 4,200 million. Is the bank compliant with the SBB/95/2025 total capital minimum?
exam.explain: 4,200 / 40,000 is 10.5%, below the 11% minimum.

exam.q: Which asset adds the least to risk-weighted assets under SBB/95/2025?
exam.explain: Birr sovereign exposures carry 0%; mortgages 35%; unrated corporates 100%.

exam.q: Total capital is Birr 6,000 million. Three companies with the same owners borrow Birr 700, 600 and 400 million. What is the position?
options: Not a large exposure, as each loan is below 10%
A breach: Birr 1,700 million is 28.3% against a 25% limit
A breach only if one loan exceeds 25%
exam.explain: Connected companies form one group; 1,700 / 6,000 is 28.3%, above the 25% limit of Birr 1,500 million.

exam.q: Total capital is Birr 6,000 million. What is the most the bank may lend to all related parties together?
exam.explain: SBB/88/2024 caps aggregate related-party exposure at 35%, which is Birr 2,100 million.

exam.q: A Birr 8 million loan is 400 days past due and fully secured by a house. What minimum provision applies?
exam.explain: 360 days or more is loss at 100%; collateral does not change the classification.

exam.q: A customer has two loans: Birr 3 million is 120 days past due and Birr 9 million is current. What happens under the cross-default rule?
options: Only the Birr 3 million loan is non-performing
Both loans are reclassified, as 25% of the exposure is non-performing
exam.explain: Birr 3 million is 25% of Birr 12 million, above the 20% trigger, so all the customer's loans are reclassified.

exam.q: A bank's IFRS impairment is Birr 900 million but the SBB/90/2024 minimum is Birr 1,050 million. What must it do?
options: Move Birr 150 million to a regulatory reserve
Write off Birr 1,050 million of loans
exam.explain: Where IFRS provisions fall short of the directive minimum, the difference goes to a regulatory reserve.

exam.q: A customer splits Birr 1.5 million of cash into many deposits at different branches. A colleague says that is legal because each deposit is small. What is the best response?
options: Refuse all future deposits and tell the customer about the report
Report the pattern to compliance for a possible STR to the FIS, without telling the customer
exam.explain: Structuring to avoid thresholds is a red flag. Compliance decides on the FIS report and the customer is not tipped off.

exam.q: Which situation is mapped correctly?
options: A firm applying for a broker licence: NBE
A customer wanting to pay a supplier in crypto: banned without NBE permission under Art. 37 of Proc. 1359/2025
A bank planning a 7% stake in an insurer: within SBB/92/2024
A loan 60 days past due: substandard
exam.explain: Brokers go to ECMA, insurer stakes are capped at 5% under SBB/92/2024, and 60 days past due is special mention.
